description: MoD's PDC is the accounting segment covering delivery of military capability (personnel · equipment · infrastructure · R&D · operations). This £5B line captures the **non-sub-allocated residual** at the PDC parent once named sub-lines (Service Personnel · Defence Nuclear Enterprise · Equipment Support · Infrastructure · Civilian Personnel · Other Costs and Services) are assigned. Best interpreted as cross-cutting/unprogrammed capability spend + centralised enablers.
notes: **Persistent Equipment Plan unaffordability**. Ajax delays + safety concerns (resolved 2023-24). Inflation eroding real-terms defence uplifts. Recruitment/retention shortfalls across services. Parent PDC entry complements specific PDC sub-lines already covered as Tier A. Persistent Equipment Plan unaffordability — first NAO unaffordable rating in 12yrs triggered PAC + Defence Committee hearings 2024. Ajax delays + safety concerns (vibration, noise) resolved 2023-24 following Defence Committee 'It is broke' report. Inflation erodes real-terms defence uplifts; Labour Jul 2024 2.5% GDP path to be sequenced via SDR. Strategic Defence Review (Healey, commissioned Jul 2024) reports Spring 2025.

description: DHSC-direct capital funding line covering NHS infrastructure · equipment · digital investment that sits OUTSIDE the main NHS England revenue envelope (~£83B for commissioning). Captures New Hospital Programme · RAAC remediation · PFI legacy charges · medical equipment capital · Community Diagnostic Centres · IT/digital transformation · ICB capital envelopes distributed to acute · mental health · community trusts. Distinct from NHSE commissioning revenue because capital is budgeted separately in HMT's CDEL framework.
notes: **NHP credibility collapse**: NAO (2023) + HSJ investigations found Boris Johnson's 40 'new' hospitals included refurbishments + wing replacements, not whole hospitals. **RAAC scandal (2023)**: 7 hospitals structurally unsafe due to 1960s-80s aerated concrete · emergency propping required. **PFI windfall**: Centre for Health and Public Interest estimated PFI consortia will extract ~£80B in unitary charges over contract lifetimes for ~£12B original construction value. **Palantir FDP contract**: controversial given US defence/intelligence ties · challenged by openDemocracy + Foxglove Legal 2023-24. NHP reset (May 2023 + Jan 2025 Labour review) confirmed only 28 of 40 original 'new hospitals' deliverable by 2030 on current budget; 5 RAAC hospitals prioritised. NAO Jul 2023 judged programme unaffordable at original £20B envelope. DHSC 2024-25 capital DEL £11.5B with £2.3B earmarked NHP. Maintenance backlog (high-risk component) £2.4B and rising.

description: **Research and Development Expenditure Credit (RDEC)** — HMRC's above-the-line taxable credit historically aimed at large companies undertaking qualifying R&D. Sits under HMRC line 4.1 (personal tax credits + corporate reliefs scored as expenditure). **From 1 April 2024 RDEC was merged with the SME scheme into a single unified R&D credit regime under Finance Act 2024**, though legacy-year claims continue under old rules.
notes: **HoC Treasury Committee + NAO flagged scale of SME fraud** (£1.04B, 2020-21). Concerns over advisor-led 'push' claim mills · IFS critiques of poor cost-benefit evidence on additionality. The merger + intensity threshold changes reshape incentives materially. **Fiscal trajectory**: cost rose from £5.2B (2021-22) to £8.1B (2023-24 provisional) — driven by 20% rate post-April 2023 + merged-scheme transition. **Take-up**: ~2.3% of active UK companies claim; FTSE350 take-up estimated 60-70%. **NAO Feb 2024** flagged £1.04B SME fraud (2020-21) as principal reform driver. **Predecessor**: replaced 2002 super-deduction model via FA 2013; merged into unified regime April 2024.

description: Funding for nationally-commissioned tertiary specialist NHS trusts providing highly complex services (cancer · cardiothoracic · paediatric · neuroscience · ophthalmology · burns · orthopaedic · women's health) requiring concentrated expertise + volumes beyond what district general hospitals can sustain. Commissioned primarily by NHS England Specialised Commissioning under the 'Prescribed Specialised Services' framework, with partial delegation to ICBs since 2022 reforms.
notes: **Tavistock GIDS closure**: Cass Review final report (April 2024) led to dissolution of Gender Identity Development Service + Tavistock & Portman trust itself · ongoing political dispute about successor regional services. **GOSH historical cases**: Charlie Gard (2017) + Archie Battersbee (2022) end-of-life cases drew international scrutiny over life-support withdrawal. **Specialist trust merger debate**: clinicians argue standalone specialist trusts preserve expertise · NHSE has pushed 'group' models + acute integration for efficiency. **Postcode variation**: delegation to ICBs raises concerns about uneven access to highly specialised care. Cass Review (final Apr 2024) led to dissolution of Tavistock GIDS — replaced by regional CYP Gender Services (London + North West) under NHS England review. Cancer specialist trusts (Royal Marsden, Christie) delivered 97% of trust-level 62-day standards vs ~65% acute average (CancerResearch UK 2024). Specialised commissioning reform subject to ongoing ICB readiness assessment.

description: Home Office system to receive, accommodate and decide asylum claims under the 1951 Refugee Convention. Includes initial accommodation, dispersed accommodation, contingency hotels, decision-making casework, appeals support, and (until July 2024) the Rwanda removal scheme.
notes: Rwanda scheme cancelled by Labour on 6 July 2024 (PM Starmer's second day). Total sunk cost ~£700M (£290M paid to Rwanda + £240M running costs + processing + legal fees) — zero removals occurred. Safety of Rwanda Act being repealed. Bibby Stockholm barge (Portland, Aug 2023-Nov 2024): Legionella found days after arrival; suicide of Leonard Farruku Dec 2023. Manston overcrowding Oct-Nov 2022 (4,000 in a 1,600-capacity site) led to diphtheria outbreak. Delivers statutory functions under Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 s.95 (support) + Asylum and Immigration Act 2002 + Nationality and Borders Act 2022. Small-boat arrivals 2024: ~36,800 (vs 29,437 in 2023). Bibby Stockholm barge closed Jan 2025. Hotel use for asylum seekers peaked ~56,000 Sept 2023, fell to ~38,000 by Oct 2024. Labour 5-year target: clear legacy backlog, process claims within 6 months, return rate to pre-2010 norms.

description: COFOG 3.6 is the residual 'not elsewhere classified' bucket for public order and safety under UN SNA 2008 — capturing functions that do not fit 3.1 police, 3.2 fire, 3.3 courts, 3.4 prisons, or 3.5 R&D. In the UK this code carries counter-terrorism operations + CONTEST strategy delivery (Prevent, Pursue, Protect, Prepare), Action Counters Terrorism campaigns, cybercrime programmes run through the NCA and NCSC, border security residuals, and the Identity and Passport Service legacy tail. Cross-government: Home Office is primary (~70%), with Cabinet Office (via NCSC), MoJ, and MoD counter-terrorism contributions.
notes: COFOG 3.6 under UN SNA 2008 is the residual 'public order and safety not elsewhere classified' code — covering administration, operation and support of activities that do not fit 3.1 through 3.5. UK sub-components comprise counter-terrorism policing grant, CONTEST strategy delivery (Prevent, Pursue, Protect, Prepare), NCSC Active Cyber Defence, border intelligence, and Martyn's Law enforcement via the SIA. The scope is cross-government across Home Office, Cabinet Office, MoJ, and MoD — whole-of-government CT envelope aggregated in the Annual CONTEST report. Revision history includes the 2018 reclassification of CTPHQ from 3.1 to 3.6 and ESA 2010 restatement for NCSC. Internationally comparable via OECD Gov at a Glance — UK 3.6 share of the 3.x total is below the EU27 average because of an integrated police model.

description: Weekly payment for people providing 35+ hours of care per week for someone who receives a qualifying disability benefit (PIP daily living, AA, or DLA middle/higher care). Taxable. The lowest of all income-replacement benefits.
notes: Overpayment scandal — The Guardian (April 2024) revealed 134,800 carers owed DWP money, ~£250M in outstanding debt, many prosecuted for earning £1–£2 over the cliff-edge £151 threshold. Labour commissioned Liz Sayce independent review (reporting 2025). The cliff-edge earnings rule — lose £1 over the threshold, lose the whole £81.90 — has been called 'indefensible' by the Work & Pensions Committee (Oct 2023). Labour's Autumn Budget 2024 raised the Carer's Allowance earnings limit from £151/wk to £196/wk (pegged to 16 hours at National Living Wage) from April 2025 — the largest rule change since CA was introduced in 1976 and a direct response to the April 2024 Guardian overpayment scandal (134,800 carers with £250M debt). Scotland replaced Carer's Allowance with Carer Support Payment (CSP) between November 2023 and April 2024, delivered by Social Security Scotland, with case-transfers complete by Spring 2025 and a unique Carer's Allowance Supplement (£288.60/yr paid in June and December) on top.

description: Resource + capital funding for rail services in Scotland: passenger operations (ScotRail + Caledonian Sleeper — BOTH now publicly owned) · Network Rail Scotland infrastructure renewals + enhancements · Transport Scotland rail capital programme · concessionary fares · rail safety/regulation contributions. Policy + most spending is devolved; Network Rail remains a UK-reserved statutory body but its Scotland route is funded through the Scottish block.
notes: **Ending peak-fares removal pilot (Sept 2024)** was criticised by unions + opposition. **ScotRail punctuality + cancellations** during driver-training + timetable-reduction periods contentious. Ongoing political question of whether public ownership has delivered promised improvements. A9/A96 dualling vs rail investment debate in climate-policy context. This is COFOG code 4.5 under UN SNA 2008, with the 'railway' of-which capturing Scottish rail — ScotRail, Caledonian Sleeper, Network Rail Scotland CP7 and Transport Scotland enhancements. Scope runs across SG, reserved DfT/Network Rail functions, and HMT fiscal-risk provisioning — a cross-government UK rail aggregate. The defining revision history item is the ONS reclassif of Network Rail INTO central government on 1 Sept 2014 under ESA10, which added ~£30B/yr to public-spending series. International comparability per OECD Gov at a Glance shows UK rail % GDP broadly in line with peers, below France (SNCF).

description: Ten regional trusts running 999 emergency response, NHS 111, patient transport, and hazardous-area response across England. Operate the Category 1–4 response model with nationally-set response-time targets.
notes: Category 2 performance collapsed winter 2022-23 due to hospital handover delays (crews stuck outside A&E). £150M+ additional funding and '45-min handover rule' introduced 2023-24. description: Non-departmental public body created in 1996 (Environment Act 1995). Regulator and operator responsible for flood & coastal risk management in England, water resources, environmental permitting, fisheries, contaminated land, and climate-adaptation advice.
notes: Sewage crisis — EA accused of under-enforcement: between 2016-2021 only 7 prosecutions vs tens of thousands of spills. OEP (Office for Environmental Protection) issued formal information notice to DEFRA/Ofwat/EA in 2023. EA budget for environmental-protection work fell ~50% real terms 2010-2020, correlating with declining river-quality monitoring. Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 gives EA power to block bonuses at failing firms and impose unlimited civil penalties. Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 (24 Feb 2025) gives EA power to impose unlimited civil penalties + block water-company executive bonuses at failing firms + new severe-pollution offences (up to 2 years imprisonment). Duffy announced Sep 2024 re-prioritisation: bigger environmental-crime task force + reduced non-statutory climate advisory work.

description: COFOG 6.2 captures administration and operation of community-development policy under UN SNA 2008 — urban and rural programmes aimed at community amenity, regeneration, and place-based economic capacity. UK scope comprises the UK Shared Prosperity Fund (post-Brexit successor to EU Structural Funds), Levelling Up Fund rounds, Towns Fund, Community Ownership Fund, Long-Term Plan for Towns, and the capital grant portion of social housing delivery. MHCLG is the primary sponsor; DCMS contributes community-arts strands and DEFRA rural community lines.
notes: COFOG 6.2 under UN SNA 2008 is 'community development' — policy administration and operation of community and urban/rural amenity programmes. UK sub-components comprise UK Shared Prosperity Fund (People & Skills / Place / Supporting Local Business), Levelling Up Fund three rounds, Towns Fund, Long-Term Plan for Towns, Community Ownership Fund, and Rural England Prosperity Fund. The scope is cross-government across MHCLG (primary), DCMS, DEFRA, and Cabinet Office — whole-of-government place-based spend. Revision history includes the 2014 housing association reclassification between 6.1 and 6.2, and PESA 2022 restatement after UKSPF replaced EU ERDF/ESF. Internationally comparable via OECD Gov at a Glance — UK 6.2 spend as % GDP is below France and Germany reflecting the UK's centralised English governance model.

description: The surviving strand of Housing Benefit covering renters who have reached State Pension age. Since UC is working-age, pensioner renters do NOT claim UC housing element — they continue through HB administered by LAs on behalf of DWP. Pension Credit claimants are passported to full HB · State Pension age renters above PC thresholds can still qualify on own means-tested basis. Caseload stable ~£3.5-4B for a decade — UC rollout did not touch it.
notes: **PC take-up gap (~37%)** became politically charged after **2024 Winter Fuel Payment means-testing** tied WFP to PC receipt — tying it to the same under-claim problem that already denies pensioner HB to eligible renters. Age UK + JRF + Independent Age argued the design relies on a gateway benefit that a third of entitled pensioners don't claim. **Structural complexity vs UC's simplification promise**: UC consolidated six working-age benefits into one, but pensioners now navigate State Pension + PC (Guarantee + Savings) + pensioner HB + Council Tax Reduction + (means-tested) WFP — arguably MORE fragmented than the post-UC working-age system. **Mixed-age couple rule (15 May 2019)**: criticised by Age UK as removing a meaningful income floor for couples with one younger partner — DWP estimated some couples lost several thousand £/year by being pushed to UC rather than pensioner HB + PC. **Over-75 free TV licence** was made contingent on PC receipt in August 2020 — reinforcing PC as a gateway benefit while also raising stakes of the PC take-up gap. Pensioner HB survives as the ONLY means-tested housing support route for pensioner renters — they cannot claim UC. Labour's Autumn Budget 2024 deferred the long-planned Pension Credit / Housing Benefit merger ('Housing Credit') from 2025 to 2028. Notable 2024 policy incoherence: pensioners on HB alone do NOT qualify for the means-tested Winter Fuel Payment (only PC does), prompting Age UK and Independent Age to lobby for HB → auto-passport to WFP. Administered by LAs (Scotland, Wales, England) and NIHE (NI); regulations identical across GB.

description: COFOG 9.2 covers secondary education (ISCED 2-3): funding for state-funded secondary schools + 16-19 provision. **CAVEAT**: the majority of English secondary school funding flows via the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) schools block through LAs + academy trusts (already captured under other lines). The £3.25B DfE-direct residual is supplementary — 16-19 capital · academy growth · T-Levels · sixth-form colleges · specific grants. Wales (DSG-equivalent via RSG) + NI (Education Authority block) operate separate devolved systems.
notes: **NI academic selection debate** (legal + social equity). **Teacher retention crisis** in England: ~13% NQTs leave within one year (DfE). **Academy trust financial failures + rebrokering cases**. **PISA 2022 maths decline** prompted curriculum debates. **RAAC school closures** issue peaked Aug-Sept 2023 · continues affecting ~230+ English schools (some secondary). **Made-for-Wales GCSE replacements** from 2025 first teaching. This is COFOG code 9.2 under UN SNA 2008, capturing secondary education (ISCED 2-3). Scope runs across DfE, LAs, the academy trust system and devolved administrations — a cross-government schools function. The series was revised under ESA10 (2014) when academy trusts were reclassif as public-sector bodies (~£20B/yr moved into central-government sub-sector), and again Nov 2022 when FE colleges were reclassif into central government. International comparability via OECD Gov at a Glance: UK secondary spend % GDP sits in line with OECD average, below Nordic peers but above southern Europe.

description: Non-departmental public body regulating English higher education. Established under Higher Education and Research Act 2017 (HERA), operational since April 2018. Single regulator for HE providers registered on the OfS Register — combines former HEFCE teaching-grant functions with market-regulation and student-protection powers. Most of the £3.18B budget flows through as teaching grants to providers; OfS's own operating cost is ~£30M. Research funding flows separately via Research England (part of UKRI).
notes: **HE sector financial crisis is the defining 2024-25 story** — OfS May 2024 Financial Sustainability report that ~40% of providers forecast deficit widely reported · mass redundancies across Sheffield · Kent · Goldsmiths · Huddersfield · Lincoln · Coventry · Newcastle and many others (UCU tracker). **Sir David Behan interim review July 2024** — OfS pivoting toward financial-sustainability monitoring as top priority. **New permanent Chair Edward Peck** appointed 2024-25. **Pause of new provider registrations** Dec 2023 extended through 2024 to focus capacity on financial monitoring. **Jan 2024 dependant visa restriction for taught PG** driving international income shock — combined with Home Office January 2024 five-measure legal-migration package (student dependant ban). **Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023** commencement paused by Labour July 2024 then partially revived — ongoing regulatory uncertainty. **David Behan review criticised OfS** for over-broad remit and under-focus on core regulatory objectives. Peck's October 2024 letter to providers paused new registration + Transparency Condition B3 enforcement while Behan Review conclusions (July 2024 independent review of OfS by Sir David Behan) were implemented. Education Sec Phillipson + Skills Minister Jacqui Smith issued formal Strategic Priorities Grant letter Nov 2024 prioritising financial sustainability + fair access + protecting freedom of speech (in post-Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023 paused regime).

description: **SMP is a statutory entitlement paid by employers to qualifying employees during maternity leave**. Employers recover 92% of SMP costs from HMRC (103% for 'small employers' under the Small Employers' Relief threshold · plus compensation for employer NICs). The DWP-paid **Maternity Allowance (MA)** is a parallel benefit for those ineligible for SMP. The budget line consolidates HMRC SMP recoveries + DWP MA outlays.
notes: **Replacement rate ~£184/week is WELL BELOW National Living Wage** for full-time hours · drives poverty among new mothers. Self-employed parents under MA lack the 90% AWE first-six-weeks. Gender pay gap implications of differential parental leave uptake. Employment Rights Bill 2024 day-one rights would eliminate 26-week qualifying period. SMP is a RESERVED employment-law benefit under the Employment Rights Act 1996 and Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 Part XII — UK-wide, no devolved equivalent (NI has mirror legislation). Employers recover 92% of SMP cost from HMRC (103% for Small Employers' Relief). Labour's Employment Rights Bill (October 2024) proposes Day-1 protections from unfair dismissal and flexible working as default — SMP qualifying-earnings / 26-week continuous-service test under consultation 2025. Maternity Allowance (MA) provides the self-employed parallel route but lacks the 90% AWE first-six-weeks uplift.

description: The **SME R&D tax relief scheme** — historically the more generous of the two UK R&D reliefs, offering an enhanced corporation tax deduction + payable tax credit for loss-makers. Merged into the unified scheme from 1 April 2024 for most claimants, with an **Enhanced R&D-Intensive SME (ERIS)** route retained for loss-making SMEs spending ≥30% of total expenditure on R&D.
notes: **Large-scale fraud + error drove HMRC's most significant overhaul of a tax relief in a decade**. Claim-mill advisors subject to HMRC enforcement. IFS + PAC criticism of limited additionality evidence. Complaints from genuine SMEs about defensive-HMRC compliance delays. **Fiscal trajectory**: SME line COMPRESSED from £4.6B (2021-22) to £3.3B (2023-24) — policy design to shrink via rate cut + AIF + intensity gating. **Take-up ~1% of SMEs** heavily concentrated in STEM sectors. **Predecessor**: FA 2000 original enhanced deduction; 2002 payable credit; rate-cut April 2023; merged April 2024 with ERIS retained. **Market**: HMRC enabler penalties tackling claim-mill abuse.

description: Defence research · science · technology line. Core delivery: **Dstl (Defence Science and Technology Laboratory)** — MoD executive agency at Porton Down — supported by **Defence and Security Accelerator (DASA)**, science + technology funding flowing through DE&S to industry primes + universities, and capability-specific R&D within programmes like GCAP · AUKUS Pillar 2 · hypersonics.
notes: **NAO/PAC critique**: MoD S&T spend has historically UNDERPERFORMED the 1.2% target — repeated findings in 'Improving the Performance of Major Defence Equipment Contracts' (2021). Ajax programme scrutiny (though procurement not R&D) shaped Defence Equipment Plan credibility debates that spilled into R&D governance. **Defence Command Paper Refresh 2023** prioritised AI · autonomy · space · cyber R&D within S&T spend. This is COFOG code 2.4 under UN SNA 2008, capturing defence research and development. Sub-components comprise Dstl, DASA, NATO research and AUKUS Pillar-2 R&D. Scope runs across MoD (lead), DSIT (dual-use), FCDO (AUKUS) and UKRI co-funded calls — a cross-government defence-science function. The defining revision history item was ESA10's (2014) reclassif of military R&D as gross fixed capital formation rather than intermediate consumption — a major UN SNA 2008 change that restated the series in Blue Book 2014.

description: **Residual Tax Credits (Working Tax Credit + Child Tax Credit) payments** during managed migration to Universal Credit. Line captures run-off payments · transitional protection top-ups · overpayment adjustments during wind-down. **Tax Credits officially closed 5 April 2025** — system ended after 23 years (Tax Credits Act 2002).
notes: **NAO 'Managing tax debts' (July 2024)** highlighted Tax Credits overpayment debts held for years with low recovery. Charities (Citizens Advice · CPAG) raised concerns about migration cliff-edge — **~20% of early Migration Notice recipients did not claim UC in time**. HMRC helpline service levels criticised by PAC. End of a 23-year benefit that Gordon Brown introduced in 2003. **Fiscal trajectory**: £12.4B (2021-22) → <£0.1B (2024-25) — 99% collapse via UC migration; residual line captures run-off + transitional protection + overpayment recovery. **Take-up pre-closure**: ~65% CTC / ~50% WTC — persistent under-claim. **Predecessor**: FC + DWA (1999 WFTC + DPTC) replaced by TCA 2002 effective April 2003. **Providers**: HMRC Tax Credits Office Preston/Washington + DWP Move-to-UC teams; no private administrator.

description: **Scotland's Affordable Housing Supply Programme (AHSP)** delivered via More Homes Division · grant-funded delivery of social rent · mid-market rent · low-cost home ownership homes through Registered Social Landlords + councils. Sits within **Housing to 2040 strategy**.

The £2.53B here is the DfE-direct component: primary-specific central programmes · PE + Sport Premium (primary-only) · primary-specific capital · targeted recruitment · residual grants.
notes: **Ruth Perry inquest (Dec 2023)** found Ofsted inspection 'likely contributed' to headteacher's suicide at Caversham Primary → triggered single-word judgement removal + Ofsted 'Big Listen' review 2024. **London primary closures**: Southwark, Lambeth, Hackney closing/amalgamating — equality concerns over concentration in high-FSM areas. **Curriculum and Assessment Review** launched by Labour July 2024 (Prof Becky Francis chair) · interim Mar 2025 · may reshape SATs/KS2. **Labour Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill (Dec 2024)** removes mandatory academisation for 'coasting' primaries — challenged by Confederation of School Trusts. This is COFOG code 9.1 under UN SNA 2008, with the 'primary' of-which capturing ISCED 1 primary-phase schooling. Scope runs across DfE, LAs, MATs and devolved admins — a cross-government schools function. The series was revised under ESA10 (2014) when primary academies were reclassif into central-government sub-sector from LG, and again following the DfE/DCSF reorganisation. International comparability via OECD Gov at a Glance: UK primary % GDP sits in line with OECD average, with higher per-pupil spend but similar aggregate scale.

description: **Low Carbon Contracts Company Ltd (LCCC)** — private company limited by shares wholly owned by the Secretary of State for DESNZ. Created 2014 under Electricity Market Reform as the SINGLE COUNTERPARTY for Contracts for Difference (CfDs) — the UK's principal mechanism for supporting low-carbon electricity generation. Issues CfD contracts · reconciles payments between generators + licensed electricity suppliers via Supplier Obligation levy · since 2023 extended to administer **Dispatchable Power Agreements** (DPAs) for power CCUS + **Hydrogen Production Business Model** contracts under Energy Act 2023. Wholly-owned subsidiary **Electricity Settlements Company (ESC)** administers the Capacity Market.
notes: **AR5 offshore wind failure (Sept 2023)** provoked industry alarm (RenewableUK · SSE · Ørsted). DESNZ responded with 66% budget uplift for AR6 + raised maximum offshore wind strike price to £73/MWh — critics argued taxpayer/billpayer absorbs the delay cost to Clean Power 2030 targets. **Mandate expanded Sept 2023**: counterparty for first **Hydrogen Allocation Round (HAR1)** — 11 projects · £2B over 15 years — + Track-1 CCUS (Net Zero Teesside). AR7 (2025) relaxed permitted-reduction mechanism. AR6 (2024) allocated record 9.6GW across 131 projects including 3.3GW fixed offshore wind + 400MW floating offshore wind — recovered from AR5 (Sept 2023) failure. AR7 expected 2025. Contracts for Difference Electricity Market Reform (EMR) 2024 white paper proposed zonal pricing — consultation ongoing. LCCC also administers Supplier Obligation reconciliation + Capacity Market counterparty functions.

description: **Proposed twin-unit EPR nuclear power station** on the Suffolk coast adjacent to operating Sizewell B (PWR) + decommissioning Sizewell A (Magnox). Project co **Sizewell C Limited** is owned via **Sizewell C (Holding) Limited**, with HMG (DESNZ + National Wealth Fund pathway) now majority shareholder alongside EDF + third-party investors. **Tree has 2 nodes (Holding + Limited) totalling £3.75B for 2024-25** — HMG equity injections + development spending ahead of **Final Investment Decision expected 2025**.
notes: **FID status at 2026-04-20 pending** — Labour Chancellor Rachel Reeves' first Budget (Oct 2024) confirmed continuation of Conservative £5.5B commitment; Great British Nuclear reorganised 2024-25 alongside NWF financing pathway. **RAB model opposition**: Citizens Advice + Which? argue the charge transfers construction-risk overruns onto billpayers before a single MW generated — risk illustrated by Hinkley C cost doubling. Environmental objections: coastal erosion · marine sanctuary · freshwater supply. **PAC**: no published 'affordability envelope' for nuclear vs renewables. FID pending at 2026-04-20. Rachel Reeves Oct 2024 Budget confirmed Conservative £5.5B commitment; Great British Nuclear restructuring 2024-25. CGN (Chinese state) exit from Sizewell C agreed 2022. RAB consumer levy expected ~£1/week on bills in construction. Hinkley Point C cost ceiling revised to £46B (2024 prices) Jan 2024 — pressure-point for Sizewell C cost estimate.

description: COFOG 5.6 is the residual 'not elsewhere classified' bucket for environmental protection under UN SNA 2008 — covering functions not captured by 5.1 waste, 5.2 wastewater, 5.3 pollution abatement, 5.4 biodiversity, or 5.5 R&D. UK scope comprises Environment Agency non-flood functions, Marine Management Organisation operating costs, Natural England non-biodiversity advisory work, cross-department climate monitoring, environmental-standards research via UKRI-NERC, and Office for Environmental Protection oversight. Spread across DEFRA, DESNZ, and DSIT with DEFRA as primary sponsor.
notes: COFOG 5.6 under UN SNA 2008 is 'environment protection not elsewhere classified' — residual category for administration, operation, and support of environmental protection activities not covered in 5.1–5.5. UK sub-components comprise Environment Agency non-flood functions, Marine Management Organisation, UKRI-NERC research, Natural England non-biodiversity advisory, and Office for Environmental Protection oversight. The scope is cross-government across DEFRA (primary), DSIT (UKRI-NERC), DESNZ (climate monitoring), and Cabinet Office — whole-of-government environmental oversight. Revision history includes the 2020 reclassification of offshore wind licensing to 4.3, ESA 2010 EA flood reclassification, and PESA 2023 OEP restatement. Internationally comparable via OECD Gov at a Glance — UK COFOG 05 total ~0.4% GDP, mid-table among OECD, below Germany and France.

key: 4.2 of which: other agriculture, food and fisheries policy
description: NI post-EU agricultural support spending administered by **DAERA** (Department of Agriculture · Environment and Rural Affairs). Successor to CAP Pillar 1 direct payments + Pillar 2 rural development · redesigned under UK Agricultural Transition + NI Future Agricultural Policy framework. Flagship schemes: Beef Carbon Reduction · Farming with Nature · Sustainable Agriculture Programme.
notes: **Lough Neagh algal blooms (2023-24)** linked in part to agricultural nutrient run-off · triggering political dispute over DAERA's Nutrients Action Programme + farm slurry spreading rules. **Sustainable Agriculture Programme** launched 2025 replacing BPS. This is COFOG code 4.2 under UN SNA 2008, with the 'other agriculture, food and fisheries policy' of-which covering NI's post-CAP DAERA support. Sub-components comprise FSTP, Sustainable Farming Programme, TB eradication, fisheries quota management and Windsor Framework agri-food admin. Scope runs across DAERA, Defra (reserved trade policy), FCDO and HMT — a cross-government NI agriculture function. The defining revision history item is the Brexit reclassif of CAP receipts from EU-transfer to UK-exchequer funding. International comparability: OECD Gov at a Glance + Producer Support Estimate show UK below OECD average.

description: COFOG 5.3 captures direct pollution-abatement spending under UN SNA 2008 — administration, operation, and support of activities reducing air, water, soil, and noise pollution. UK scope comprises Clean Air Zone funding, DEFRA air-quality grant, EA water-quality monitoring and Nitrate Vulnerable Zone enforcement, UK Emissions Trading Scheme administration, industrial-emissions regulation, vehicle-emissions capex (OZEV plug-in grants legacy tail), and the pollution-reduction fraction of Net Zero delivery. DESNZ is primary for climate; DEFRA for air and water; DfT for vehicle emissions.
notes: COFOG 5.3 under UN SNA 2008 is 'pollution abatement' — administration and operation of activities that prevent, reduce, treat, and eliminate pollution of air, water, soil, and noise. UK sub-components comprise Clean Air Zones, DEFRA air-quality grant, EA water monitoring and NVZ enforcement, UK ETS administration, industrial-emissions regulation, OZEV vehicle-emissions legacy, and the pollution-reduction fraction of Net Zero delivery. The scope is cross-government across DESNZ, DEFRA, DfT, and devolved administrations — whole-of-government abatement spend. Revision history includes the 2018 reclassification of UK ETS admin from 4.3 to 5.3, PESA 2022 storm-overflows restatement, and 2023 Net Zero split clarification. Internationally comparable via OECD PAC expenditure accounts — UK 5.3 ~0.07% GDP, below France and Germany.

description: DfT funding for buses · light rail · trams in England outside London (TfL separate). Bus Service Operators Grant (BSOG) fuel rebate · concessionary fares via ENCTS · bus franchising/enhanced-partnership support under Bus Services Act 2017 + **Better Buses Bill 2024** · capital grants to light rail systems.
notes: **Raising fare cap £2→£3 (50% rise) Jan 2025** drew criticism from Campaign for Better Transport as hitting low-income rural users hardest. **Franchising transition in GM** was challenged (unsuccessfully) by Stagecoach in 2022 judicial review. **Buses Bill 2024** removes 2017 restriction preventing new municipal bus companies · enabling authorities to set up own operators. The series was revised under ESA10 (2014) when TfL was reclassif as an NDPB inside central government, and again after the Bus Services Act 2017 franchising reforms. International comparability via OECD Gov at a Glance: UK broadly in line with OECD average, below France/Germany.

description: Residual DfT spend covering maritime · ports · aviation · freight · internal DfT running costs. Major components: **Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA)** · Air Accidents Investigation Branch · Marine Accident Investigation Branch · port infrastructure schemes · freight decarbonisation.
notes: **P&O Ferries mass-sacked 786 seafarers** March 2022 without consultation — exposed gaps in UK maritime employment law. **Seafarers' Wages Regulations** came into force late 2024 after scandal · requiring ferries calling UK ports ≥120 times/yr to pay NMW-equivalent in UK waters (criticised by unions as too narrow). **Freeports** criticised by IFS + Centre for Cities as risk of displacement rather than additional growth. This is COFOG code 4.5 under UN SNA 2008, with the 'other transport' of-which covering maritime, aviation, ports, freight and DfT central running costs — the transport-function residual. The series was revised under ESA10 (2014) following MCA agency reclassif and ports-authority boundary restatement, and again after the Seafarers' Wages Act 2023. International comparability via OECD Gov at a Glance: UK aviation+maritime % GDP sits below OECD average, reflecting privatised UK ports vs state-owned port peers in France and Spain.

description: Top-up grant paid to English schools for disadvantaged pupils — designed to narrow the attainment gap. Eligibility: pupils registered for Free School Meals at any point in the last 6 years ('Ever 6 FSM'), looked-after and previously looked-after children, and service children.
notes: Rates rose only ~1.5% for 2024-25 despite ~6% wage inflation — real-terms cut. Sutton Trust and EEF research show the disadvantage gap widened post-pandemic to the highest level in a decade. Critics argue the 'Ever 6' metric misses families just above the FSM threshold (~£7,400 household income cap). Pupil Premium has lost ~20% real value since 2015. PP is England-only — Scotland's equivalent is Pupil Equity Funding (PEF, £130M, £1,320/pupil via Curriculum for Excellence); Wales has the Pupil Development Grant (PDG, £130M); Northern Ireland has no direct analogue (relies on needs-based LA formula). Real-terms value has fallen ~13% since 2015 (EPI/Sutton Trust). Labour's Child Poverty Strategy is due Spring 2025 (joint Phillipson/Kendall) and is expected to consider both expanding FSM auto-enrolment (~200k additional Ever6 pupils) and re-purposing the PP envelope to align with a broader child-poverty framework.

description: UNFUNDED government-operated scheme holding the **historical pension liabilities of Royal Mail employees accrued BEFORE 1 April 2012** — when HMG assumed obligations from the Royal Mail Pension Plan (RMPP) to permit Royal Mail's privatisation. Administered by Capita on behalf of Cabinet Office / DBT · pays benefits from the Consolidated Fund. NO new accrual.
notes: **NAO + Institute for Government critique**: 2012 nationalisation of liabilities 'flattered' headline deficit figures at privatisation · ~£28B asset transfer scored as cash receipt against deficit while much longer-tailed liabilities accrued slowly in subsequent years. Post-2012 active Royal Mail pension liabilities remain in the private Royal Mail Pension Plan (funded DB section, CDC from Oct 2024 — UK's first collective defined-contribution scheme). The £1.52B RMSPS line is annual pay-out run-off; total remaining liabilities ~£30B amortising over ~50 years as cohort dies off.  Post-privatisation pension legacy split: RMSPS (Cabinet Office, pre-Apr 2012 service) vs continuing Royal Mail Pension Plan (defined benefit for plc, now closed to future accrual since 2018). Transfer into public sector delivered ~£28B assets + £37.5B liabilities to HMT as one-off transaction. Scheme is administered by MyCSP on behalf of Cabinet Office. Ofcom USO review 2024 + privatised Royal Mail takeover by EP Group (International Distribution Services, completed Apr 2025) do not affect this legacy scheme. The scheme was created on 1 April 2012 under the Postal Services Act 2011, when Royal Mail's ~450,000 pre-privatisation pension members and their £37.5B of plan assets were transferred to HM Government to enable the 2013 Royal Mail IPO free of the historic pension deficit. Administration is delivered by Capita Employee Solutions under contract to the Royal Mail Pension Plan Trustees Ltd, with Cabinet Office as scheme owner and HM Treasury as funding authority. The liability is UK-wide and fully reserved — it generates no Barnett consequentials because it is a legacy Exchequer obligation rather than a devolved service. Annual cash flow tracks CPI uprating of a closed, shrinking pensioner population.

description: **Welsh Government's internal contingency reserve** held centrally at start of year · unallocated to specific portfolio MEGs (Main Expenditure Groups). Flexibility mechanism for in-year pressures + supplementary budgets.
notes: **Welsh Fiscal Framework review (Dec 2023)** expanded drawdown flexibilities. **2025-26 budget saw LARGER than typical opening DUP** due to UK Spending Review settlement timing. description: **UK Shared Prosperity Fund** — domestic replacement for EU Structural & Investment Funds (ERDF · ESF · Cohesion) post-Brexit. Administered by MHCLG. description: Pupil Premium allocated via Local Authorities to LA-maintained schools (community · voluntary-controlled · voluntary-aided · foundation). Represents shrinking pre-academy portion of the PP envelope as academies grow.
notes: **Academy conversion rate slowed substantially 2022-2025** after 2022 Schools White Paper 'all schools in a strong trust by 2030' ambition was effectively dropped. Criticism that **PP eligibility data held at LA level is less reliable post-UC rollout**. Some LAs accused of slow pass-through to schools (cash-flow issues). PP-LA mirrors PP-Academies in all respects except the administrative channel — allocated via DfE formula on January school census Ever6 FSM flags, routed through LAs to community / VC / VA / foundation schools. Real-terms value has fallen ~13% since 2015 (EPI / Sutton Trust). Scotland's Pupil Equity Funding (PEF, £1,320/pupil) and Wales's Pupil Development Grant (PDG, £1,150/pupil) are the devolved analogues; NI has no direct equivalent. Academy conversion rates slowed substantially since the 2022 Schools White Paper 'strong-trust by 2030' ambition was dropped — under Labour's December 2024 Schools Bill, no changes to the PP envelope or routing are proposed.

description: **National Wealth Fund (NWF)** — HM Treasury-owned public financial institution established by **rebadging + expanding the UK Infrastructure Bank (UKIB) on 14 July 2024**. Despite the 'wealth fund' name, it operates as a **development bank** (closer to Germany's KfW or Brazil's BNDES) — NOT a sovereign wealth fund. Invests borrowed + appropriated public capital into commercial projects alongside private co-investors · expects a return. HQ: Leeds. £1.26B reflects net fiscal cost of loans + guarantees + equity to HMT (not total assets deployed).
notes: **Rebrand largely cosmetic critique** (IFS · Green Alliance · HoL Economic Affairs Committee): £27.8B capacity is modest vs KfW/BNDES; overlapping mandates with Great British Energy · Great British Nuclear · UK Export Finance risk duplication. **Additionality paradox** (Conservative opposition): if deals happen anyway, public capital subsidises private returns; if they wouldn't, returns are likely sub-commercial — challenging 'return to taxpayer' story. Statement of Strategic Priorities Oct 2024 added clean steel + defence-adjacent industrial capacity. Early 2025: linked to Sizewell C financing + Great British Energy co-investment pipeline. NWF 'Strategic Steer' Oct 2024 (Chancellor letter) prioritised 5 sectors: clean energy, hydrogen, CCUS, gigafactories, ports. Overlap with Great British Energy (DESNZ, £8.3B) + Great British Nuclear (DESNZ) a recurrent IfS + IFG critique. Autumn Budget 2024 confirmed NWF capitalised £27.8B. Non-debt-rule-compliant treatment (PSND ex BoE metric) key attraction for Labour's fiscal rules.

key: 4.2 of which: market support under CAP
description: COFOG 4.2 sub-line capturing residual market-support payments under the legacy Common Agricultural Policy regime — Basic Payment Scheme (BPS) delinked payments and run-off of Pillar 1 direct support to English farmers post-Brexit. Under the UN SNA 2008 classification this sits inside agriculture, forestry and fishing (4.2). DEFRA is the primary sponsor (~95%), with devolved administrations (Scottish Government, Welsh Government, DAERA Northern Ireland) operating parallel schemes. The UK has been running down CAP-inherited payments from 2021, transitioning to Environmental Land Management (ELMs) and Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI).
notes: Delivery sits with the Rural Payments Agency (RPA), DEFRA's executive agency. DEFRA's Farming and Countryside Programme drives the BPS→ELM transition under DEFRA Permanent Secretary Tamara Finkelstein. The Labour Autumn Budget 2024 kept the £2.4B/yr ELM envelope ring-fenced but introduced an Inheritance Tax agricultural property relief cap (£1M from April 2026) that triggered tractor protests in Westminster November 2024. NAO 2024 'Farming and Countryside Programme' review flagged lag in ELM uptake relative to the BPS run-off speed — cliff-edge risk for ~30% of smaller farms whose income falls faster than SFI payments ramp. CB7-style cross-compliance reforms planned 2025-26.

key: New State Pension Protected Payments (Including Inherited Elements)
description: The 'grandfathering' top-up element of the new State Pension. Preserves pre-April-2016 entitlement for those whose Starting Amount at 6 April 2016 was HIGHER than the full new State Pension rate — paid ABOVE the full nSP. Only applies to those with substantial pre-2016 SERPS/S2P entitlement (mostly middle/higher-earners with long contracted-in histories). 'Including Inherited Elements' captures spousal-inherited Additional Pension rights folded in on bereavement.
notes: **Structurally diminishing line** — no new Protected Payment entitlement can accrue after 6 April 2016, so the line shrinks as recipients pass away. Represents the 'grandfathering cost' of the single-tier transition. **IFS 2015-16 analyses** of the single-tier transition documented clear **winners and losers**: low-earners + self-employed (previously excluded from SERPS/S2P) **gained**; higher-earners with long contracted-in histories **lost relative to the counterfactual**, partially offset by Protected Payments. **CPI-only uprating** means Protected Payments erode in real terms relative to full nSP over time — a 'stealth' disadvantage for higher-earning transition retirees that was acknowledged in the 2014 Impact Assessment but receives limited public attention. The 'Inherited Elements' dimension surfaces occasionally in tribunal cases where widows/widowers contest DWP calculations of inherited Additional Pension rights. Protected Payments are a RESERVED matter UK-wide — no Scottish, Welsh or NI equivalent exists; delivered by DWP Pension Service. F&E rate matches the parent State Pension line at around 0.1% — the lowest in the DWP portfolio due to NI record-based computation. A distinctive quirk: Protected Payments are uprated by CPI only (not triple lock), under Pensions Act 2014 s.5 — so the sub-line erodes in real terms vs the headline new State Pension that enjoys the full triple lock. The line is structurally diminishing as the pre-2016 Starting Amount cohort passes away.

description: **Criminal legal aid** administered by the **Legal Aid Agency (LAA)** — MoJ executive agency since April 2013 (replaced Legal Services Commission). Funds legal representation for defendants in police stations · magistrates' courts · Crown Court · Court of Appeal meeting interests-of-justice + (most) means tests. Delivery via **Advocates Graduated Fee Scheme (AGFS)** for barristers + **Litigators Graduated Fee Scheme (LGFS)** for firms + Very High Cost Cases (VHCC) + duty solicitor rotas.
notes: **2022 Criminal Bar Association indefinite walkout** (June-September 2022) was the defining dispute — junior barristers cited real-terms income falls of ~28% since 2006. Bellamy settlement's exclusion of back-payments for existing cases prolonged action. Ongoing friction 2025-26 concerns LGFS parity + **Law Society judicial review pre-action letter over rate adequacy**. Bellamy CLAIR review (Nov 2021) recommended ≥15% minimum fee uplift for criminal solicitors + police-station work; MoJ implemented ~12-13% via Dec 2022 SI but excluded solicitors from full recommendation. Labour's Lord Chancellor Mahmood confirmed Feb 2025 additional £40M for criminal legal aid solicitors in response to CBA + Law Society concerns on backlog capacity.

key: University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust
description: Staffordshire and Shropshire tertiary teaching trust formed 1 November 2014 from the merger of University Hospital of North Staffordshire (Stoke) and Mid Staffordshire NHS FT (acquired post the Francis Inquiry — Mid Staffs was dissolved following the scandal). Runs Royal Stoke University Hospital (Stoke, Level 1 major trauma + regional cardiothoracic) and County Hospital (Stafford). Affiliated with Keele University School of Medicine.
notes: UHNM is the successor trust to the Mid Staffordshire NHS FT that was dissolved following the 2013 Francis Inquiry (one of the defining NHS care failures of the 2010s). Substantive CEO Simon Evans-Evans took over in 2024 from interim Tracy Bullock. 2023 CQC inspection rated UHNM Requires Improvement overall. FY2024-25 closed ~£55M deficit, underlying ~£85M. The Royal Stoke PFI (~£65M/yr unitary charge through 2040) is one of the largest PFI burdens outside London. Royal Stoke became a symbol of the 2024-25 corridor care crisis with widely shared images of patients in A&E corridors.

key: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
description: Devon integrated acute and community FT formed 1 April 2022 from the merger of Royal Devon and Exeter NHS FT and Northern Devon Healthcare NHS Trust. Runs the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital (Wonford), North Devon District Hospital (Barnstaple), Tiverton and District Hospital, Okehampton Hospital and a wide Devon community network. Affiliated with the University of Exeter; NIHR Exeter BRC. Covers nearly 2,000 square miles of mixed rural coastal geography.
notes: CEO Sam Higginson took over in March 2024, succeeding the architects of the 2022 merger. 2023 CQC inspection rated Royal Devon Good overall. FY2024-25 closed ~£18M deficit, underlying ~£35M — one of the better outturns among large provincial trusts. NDDH (Barnstaple) is in the New Hospital Programme for later-wave rebuild. Royal Devon is a rare true integrated acute-plus-community FT, making it a test case for the direction of NHS integrated provision.
